analysis.one_liner: Requires internet, TV, and phone companies to advertise total prices and bans forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 55 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died in subcommittee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The TRUE Fees Act would have required internet, TV, and phone providers to advertise the full price of a service, including all the company's fees. It would have required itemized electronic bills, 21 days' notice plus a penalty-free exit from a contract whenever the provider raised the price, and a freeze on equipment rental fee hikes unless the equipment was meaningfully upgraded. It also would have banned and voided contract clauses forcing customers into arbitration over billing disputes.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy internet, phone, wireless, or cable TV service. They would see the true price up front instead of a low advertised rate padded with administrative and equipment fees, could cancel without an early termination fee whenever the provider raised the price, and could take billing disputes — unexpected charges, fees for services or rentals they never signed up for — to court instead of being forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Providers could not advertise a price unless it is the total they will charge, including administrative fees, equipment rental fees, and other charges — closing the gap between the low advertised rate and the actual bill.

Electronic bills would have to arrive by email (viewable without logging into an account) and include an itemized breakdown of the base service charge versus fees and taxes, at the same detail as a paper bill.

If a provider raises the total charge by any amount, it must give clear notice at least 21 days in advance and let the customer end the contract without paying an early termination fee or other penalty.
Providers could not raise equipment rental fees unless the equipment was upgraded to give a substantial increase in functionality — targeting recurring set-top box and router fee increases.

Providers could not put forced arbitration clauses in customer contracts, and any such clause would be void and unenforceable; this covers disputes over unnotified price increases, broken promotional rates, and charges for services or equipment the customer never subscribed to or rented.

analysis.who_pays: Telecom, cable, and broadband providers (companies like the large cable, satellite, and wireless carriers) would bear the costs: redesigning advertising and billing to show all-in prices and itemized details, giving up revenue from administrative and equipment rental fees and from early termination penalties, honoring promotional rates, and losing the ability to push billing disputes into arbitration. Some of that cost could be passed back to customers through higher base prices.

drawbacks.text: The all-in advertised price does not have to include state and local taxes that are not uniform nationwide, so the advertised total could still fall short of what a customer actually pays in high-tax areas.

Because any increase — no matter how small — triggers a 21-day warning and a penalty-free exit, providers might respond by avoiding promotional discounts or locking in fewer short-term deals, and compliance costs could be passed on in higher base prices.

The bill bans arbitration clauses only for the specific billing disputes it defines; a customer in arbitration over those issues loses a channel some providers argue is faster and cheaper than court, though it is one the company typically chooses and pays for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gains are real and concrete: an honest advertised price, itemized bills, the ability to walk away from a contract when the price goes up, and court access for billing disputes. The costs are compliance spending by providers and some risk that promotional pricing becomes less generous or base rates rise. The most notable design gap is the carve-out for non-uniform state and local taxes, which keeps a piece of the advertised-price problem unfixed. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the costs, though the bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on February 14, 2019 with nine original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, where it stayed.
Fifty-five House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, but no Republicans did, and the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still parked in subcommittee, so it died and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable, internet, and wireless providers are better off: they keep the current billing system — low advertised rates padded with administrative and equipment fees, price increases without penalty-free exits, and contract clauses that push billing disputes into arbitration.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to measure party positions, but all 55 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, while the Democratic-led committee never acted on the bill either.

industries.note: The bill attacks the core of how these companies bill customers: low advertised rates padded with administrative and equipment fees, surprise price increases, and early termination penalties. It would force all-in advertised pricing, itemized e-bills, 21-day notice with a penalty-free exit on any price increase, and an end to forced arbitration for billing disputes.
Providers charge recurring monthly rental fees on equipment the customer usually cannot avoid; the bill would freeze those fees unless the equipment receives a substantial functional upgrade.

Mandatory arbitration clauses in telecom contracts generate dispute-resolution business; the bill would prohibit such clauses in covered contracts and void any that slip in, sending covered billing disputes to court instead.
